newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court clears Berlusconi brother of plot.
newsitem.headline: Italian court clears Berlusconi brother of plot.

text.p: A court acquitted former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi's brother Paolo and his defence minister Cesare Previti on Wednesday of charges that they plotted to discredit Italy's leading anti-graft magistrate.
The court in Brescia, northern Italy, announced its verdict after retiring for two days to consider its ruling in one of the country's most perplexing trials.

Judge Francesco Maddalo told the court that Paolo Berlusconi, Previti and two other defendants, former justice ministry inspectors Ugo Dinacci and Domenico De Biase, had been acquitted because there was no case to answer.

The four had been formally charged with extortion after prosecutors alleged that they engaged in a plot to force magistrate Antonio Di Pietro, star of Italy's judicial assault on graft, to resign in December 1994.

The not guilty verdict had been expected after public prosecutor Raimondo Giustozzi, brought into the case midway through the trial after his predecessor was removed for alleged bias, called for acquittals in his summing up on January 20.
Di Pietro was the spearhead of the elite pool of "Clean Hands" magistrates in Milan whose investigations into graft since 1992 felled Italy's old governing class.

The pool announced in November 1994 that it was investigating media mogul Silvio Berlusconi, then head of a centre-right government after storming into politics at the start of the year. He is now opposition leader.

Silvio Berlusconi and his brother Paolo, a business associate, were later indicted on corruption charges in that case, which arose over alleged bribes paid to tax inspectors by companies in the Berlusconi empire.
Di Pietro, a former policeman, has never fully explained why he abruptly quit the judiciary.
He has successfully defeated allegations, some of which were aired in the Brescia trial, that he abused his position to extract financial and other favours from suspects.
Fresh investigations came to the surface last month, prompting Di Pietro to resign as public works minister, a post he was given last May.
The four defendants at the trial which ended on Wednesday had denied seeking to discredit Di Pietro.
Part of the initial prosecution case was that they used damaging allegations to force Di Pietro to resign from the Milan pool.
"My conclusions led me to recommend an acquittal. This is neither a victory nor a defeat," prosecutor Giustozzi said.
